[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] TierPoint is headquartered at 12444 Powerscourt Drive, Suite 450, in St. Louis, Missouri, and traces to 2010, when the company acquired its first data center in Dallas, Texas. Argo Infrastructure Partners increased its ownership stake and capital commitment to TierPoint in a transaction reported in December 2025, following an earlier round in which TierPoint closed $320 million in equity from a consortium of investors.

The companys own site describes a portfolio of 40 data center facilities across 20 US markets coast-to-coast, serving thousands of companies spanning small businesses to Fortune 500 enterprises across both public and private sectors.

The registry here tracks 3 TierPoint facilities across three states, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Texas, a small subset of the companys 20 named markets. TierPoints origin in a 2010 Dallas acquisition and its continued Texas presence in this registry connect it to the same Dallas-Fort Worth corridor already carrying Stream, Digital Realty, and Aligned facilities recorded elsewhere in this registry. This specific facility, recorded in this registry as TierPoint in Williamson County, TN, was not individually named in the operator-level research above; its operator field was blank in the source data and is corrected here to TierPoint based on the facility own name, which unambiguously identifies its operator brand. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
This facility publishes no power capacity, limiting any judgment of its scale relative to other Tennessee data centers or its fitness for AI training workloads.

TierPoint operates this 26,000-square-foot colocation site as a suite within a larger building rather than a purpose-built shell, which signals mid-market enterprise demand rather than hyperscale infrastructure. The seven certifications on file, dominated by SOC 1 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, HITRUST, and ITAR, describe a workload profile tilted toward compliance-driven use cases: financial systems under audit control, payment card processing, regulated healthcare data, and export-restricted defense information. ISO 27001 and LEED round out a stack that prioritizes security governance and operational standards over raw capacity.

For AI specifically, this signature matters. Large-scale GPU training requires transparent power density and sustained load capacity, neither of which this facility publishes. The certification portfolio instead suggests inference, data management, or model serving for regulated industries, where compliance overhead exceeds the computational demand of training runs. Tennessee as a whole publishes power figures for only one of twenty-four mapped facilities, making state-level pattern detection impossible. This facility's contribution to the regional AI compute base cannot be assessed from the data available.
